Expectation1: Listen actively and provide emotional support when needed.
Situation1: A friend sends a text message complaining about having a long, boring day.
Situation2: A dispatch call sends the ambulance driver through heavy city traffic to a location where a patient has a non-life-threatening injury.
Story: My phone buzzed with a message from Sam just as I was pulling out of the ambulance bay. “Rough day. Can you talk?” he wrote. I knew he needed someone to listen, to be there for him, and I wanted to be that friend. But the radio crackled, dispatch sending me to a minor accident across town. The city traffic was thick, horns blaring, drivers impatient. I gripped the wheel, focusing on weaving through the congestion, every second counting for the patient waiting. My phone vibrated again, Sam’s words lighting up the screen. I felt the tug—my friend needed me, but so did the person at the end of this drive. I couldn’t text while driving, not with lives at stake, but guilt gnawed at me for not being there for Sam. The weight of both roles pressed on me, each demanding my full attention, and I found myself caught in the middle, heart racing, unsure which responsibility to answer first.
